svg.text: FIG 06: SUBSTITUTION, COMPENSATION & TELLEGEN SENSITIVITY ENGINE
Branch Replacement Equivalence • Impedance Perturbation ΔZ • Virtual Compensation Source Vc = I·ΔZ • Network Sensitivity Analysis

g.text: 1. Substitution Theorem
Formal Statement & Physical Principle
If the voltage across and current through any branch k of an arbitrary electric
network are known to be v_k(t) and i_k(t), then that branch can be REPLACED
(substituted) by any combination of elements that maintains identical terminal
voltage or current, without altering voltages and currents in ANY OTHER branch!
1. Replace with Ideal Voltage Source: v_source(t) = v_k(t)
2. Replace with Ideal Current Source: i_source(t) = i_k(t)
3. Replace with Equivalent Resistor: R_eq = v_k / i_k
Universality: Valid for Non-Linear Networks!
Does Substitution Require Linearity?
NO! Substitution applies to LINEAR AND NON-LINEAR networks alike!
• Branch k can contain non-linear diodes, transistors, or time-varying elements.
• As long as operating point (V_k, I_k) is established, replacing it with an
independent source of value V_k or I_k preserves all remaining circuit state.
The Unique Solution Condition:
• Substitution is valid IF AND ONLY IF the network possesses a UNIQUE solution.
• Substitution fails if replacing the branch creates an all-voltage-source loop
with conflicting potentials or an all-current-source cutset with KCL violation!
Substitution Solved Classroom Drill
A bridge circuit with non-linear tunnel diode has measured terminal voltage
V_D = 0.7 V and current I_D = 15 mA.
Analysis via Substitution:
1. Remove the complex exponential diode model entirely from the schematic.
2. Substitute an ideal DC voltage source of 0.7 V in its place.
3. Now the ENTIRE network becomes completely linear!
4. Use Nodal Analysis or Superposition to solve all other branch currents in seconds.
Alternative Verification:
Replace diode with equivalent static resistance R_D = 0.7 V / 15 mA = 46.67 Ω.
Yields identically matching voltages and currents across all external resistors!
Crucial Limitations of Substitution
1. External Circuit Invariance ONLY:
Substitution preserves voltages/currents outside the substituted branch.
Internal microscopic physics and internal dynamics are NOT duplicated.
2. Power Equivalence Limitation:
Instantaneous power absorbed by substituted source v_k · i_k equals original
power, but small-signal dynamic resistance dv/di is NOT preserved!
Cannot use substituted circuit to evaluate AC small-signal variations!
2. Compensation Theorem
The Impedance Perturbation Principle
In a linear time-invariant active network, if the resistance of branch k carries an
initial current I and its resistance is changed by an increment ΔR (from R to R + ΔR),
the resulting CHANGE IN CURRENT (ΔI) in all other branches of the network
equals the current produced by an opposing virtual COMPENSATION SOURCE V_c
inserted in series with the modified branch, with all original independent sources killed:
V_c = I · ΔR (Opposing original current I!)
ΔI_branch = Response due to V_c alone
Mathematical Derivation via Substitution & Superposition
1. Original branch voltage: V = I · R.
2. Modified branch resistance: R' = R + ΔR. New current: I' = I + ΔI.
3. New branch voltage:
V' = I' · (R + ΔR) = I' · R + I' · ΔR
4. By Substitution, replace term (I' · ΔR) with an opposing voltage source:
V_c = I' · ΔR ≈ I · ΔR (for small perturbations ΔR ≪ R)
5. By Superposition, the change in currents ΔI across the network is driven
SOLEY by compensation source V_c acting in the dead network (R_th network)!
ΔI_k = -V_c / (R_th + R + ΔR) = -I · ΔR / (R_th + R + ΔR)
Compensation Solved Classroom Drill
A 5 Ω resistor carries an initial current of I = 4 A in a network where Thévenin
resistance facing the resistor terminals is R_th = 15 Ω.
If the 5 Ω resistor increases by ΔR = +1 Ω (to 6 Ω), find the new branch current I'.
Step 1: Compensation source magnitude:
V_c = I · ΔR = 4 A · 1 Ω = 4 V (opposing)
Step 2: Change in branch current:
Step 3: New actual branch current:
Solved in 45 seconds without re-solving the entire multi-loop circuit!
Primary Applications in Electrical Engineering
1. Bridge Sensitivity & Strain Gauges:
• Calculating output voltage deflection ΔV when a strain gauge undergoes
minute fractional resistance changes (ΔR/R ≈ 10⁻³).
2. Ammeter Insertion Error Analysis:
• Inserting an ammeter of internal resistance R_A adds ΔR = R_A to branch.
• Current reduction: ΔI = -I · R_A / (R_th + R_A).
3. Power Grid Fault Analysis & Line Outages:
• Modeling tripping of a transmission line (ΔR → ∞) as an injected current.
3. Network Sensitivity Formulation
Differential Sensitivity vs. Incremental Perturbation
As parameter change approaches the infinitesimal limit (ΔR → 0):
dI / dR = lim_{ΔR → 0} (ΔI / ΔR) = -I / (R_th + R)
Normalized Sensitivity (Bode's Sensitivity Index):
S_R^I = (dI / I) / (dR / R) = (R / I) · (dI / dR)
S_R^I = -R / (R_th + R)
• Dimensionless index quantifying percentage change in response per 1% change in R.
Wheatstone Bridge Deflection Sensitivity
For an initially balanced Wheatstone bridge with equal arms R driven by V_s:
When arm 1 changes by small strain ΔR (R₁ = R + ΔR):
V_th(unbalanced) = V_s · [ (R + ΔR)/(2R + ΔR) - R/2R ]
V_th ≈ V_s · (ΔR / 4R) [For ΔR ≪ R]
Bridge Sensitivity Metric:
S_B = V_out / (ΔR / R) = V_s / 4 (Volts per unit strain)
• Thévenin resistance of the bridge: R_th = (R ∥ R) + (R ∥ R) = R/2 + R/2 = R.
• Galvanometer current: I_g = V_th / (R_th + R_g) = (V_s · ΔR / 4R) / (R + R_g).
Full-Bridge Strain Sensitivity Enhancement
Comparing Bridge Configurations for Strain Sensing:
1. Quarter Bridge (1 active arm):
V_out = (V_s / 4) · (ΔR / R) ⟹ Sensitivity = 1× (Baseline)
2. Half Bridge (2 active push-pull arms +ΔR, -ΔR):
V_out = (V_s / 2) · (ΔR / R) ⟹ Sensitivity = 2× (Doubled!)
3. Full Bridge (4 active push-pull arms):
V_out = V_s · (ΔR / R) ⟹ Sensitivity = 4× (Quadrupled!)
Full Bridge Benefits: 4× sensitivity + automatic temperature cancellation!
Thermal drift affects all 4 arms equally (+ΔR_T), canceling completely at detector.
Matrix Formulation of Network Sensitivities
In systematic Nodal Analysis: [Y][V] = [I].
Differentiating with respect to parameter p:
d[V]/dp = -[Y]⁻¹ · (d[Y]/dp) · [V] (Adjoint Sensitivity!)
• Requires inverting admittance matrix [Y] only ONCE!
• Sensitivities to all N circuit components calculated via simple vector products.
Form basis of modern CAD / SPICE circuit optimization engines!
4. Tellegen & Adjoint Sensitivity
Tellegen's Theorem & Quasi-Tellegen Form
1. Tellegen's Theorem (Single Network N):
• Power conservation holds topologically regardless of linearity or components!
2. Quasi-Tellegen Theorem (Two Distinct Networks N and N'):
If N and N' share the IDENTICAL TOPOLOGICAL GRAPH but have different elements:
• Cross-products of voltages from N with currents from N' sum identically to zero!
The Adjoint Network Sensitivity Method
Director & Rohrer's Adjoint Method: Choose N' as the topologically ADJOINT network
where all non-reciprocal elements are transposed:
Sensitivity Calculation Equation:
ΔV_out = -∑_{elements} [ v_k · Δi_k' - i_k · Δv_k' ]
• For a perturbed resistor R_k: Δv_k = ΔR_k · i_k.
Sensitivity: ∂V_out / ∂R_k = -i_k · i_k'
Incredible Efficiency: A SINGLE adjoint simulation gives sensitivities
of output voltage to ALL 10,000 components in an integrated circuit!
Proof of Reciprocity via Quasi-Tellegen
Subtracting the two Quasi-Tellegen identities:
Separate branches into Port Branches (P) and Internal Resistor Branches (R):
∑_P (v_P i_P' - v_P' i_P) + ∑_R (v_R i_R' - v_R' i_R) = 0
For linear bilateral internal resistors: v_R = R · i_R and v_R' = R · i_R'.
v_R · i_R' - v_R' · i_R = (R i_R) i_R' - (R i_R') i_R ≡ 0 !
All internal terms vanish identically! Leaving only the two ports:
V₁ I₁' + V₂ I₂' = V₁' I₁ + V₂' I₂ (Q.E.D.)

Topological conservation theorems govern all electric networks!
